sections.title: How to orchestrate and track a logistics process without blind spots?
body: The wholesale logistics process was operating with blind spots. While basic systems were in place for initial order intake and storage, the intermediate transit lacked traceability.

As a team, we designed and iterated a microservices platform to orchestrate the entire lifecycle of an order, providing real-time visibility to every department without disrupting the operational flow.

sections.title: The black hole of traceability and human memory
body: Whenever products were moved from the storage area down to the consolidation zones, the digital trail vanished, largely due to the variety of item packaging. This forced consolidation operators to rely on their memory, or pickers to constantly track down the physical location of each part of an order.
Even though there was some underlying organization, the cognitive load was causing bottlenecks and accidental mix-ups of merchandise between different customer orders.

Additionally, the system had to be deployed in an environment with disparate resources. Some areas used legacy laser barcode scanners, others had newer QR readers, and some relied on touchscreens, meaning our platform had to be hardware-agnostic.

sections.title: Physical rules dictate software design
body: Our best decisions came from stepping out of the department and visiting the warehouse floor to understand their workflows and operations. We realized that physical logistics dictate software rules: for instance, while standard merchandise flowed from storage via a ramp system (with a short average transit time), massive pallet orders went down through freight elevators.
Both shared the same service, but required completely different queuing logic and configurable time averages.
We also understood the human factor: adopting a new tool is always perceived as "extra work." We needed the interface to reduce friction and provide immediate value to the operator.

blocks.text: To solve the time wasted in the Dispatch area, we implemented a visual interface that mapped out the physical layout of the warehouse. Instead of reading plain text lists, the operator saw the exact location of their order on the screen. This eliminated the need to search blindly and reduced cognitive friction.
Microservices for operational autonomy, not scalability

We structured the platform into independent microservices not for massive traffic, but for zone autonomy. If an order arrived at Consolidation without prior records, the system didn't apply a strict block; it allowed the next area to continue the process, query, or modify statuses. I personally developed the storage, ramps/elevators, and monitoring services.
The monitoring service acted as the source of truth. It worked alongside the core service to consolidate statuses and prevent different zones from interpreting an order differently.
It compiled the state "fragments" from each zone, transformed them into an immutable log, and distributed the changes in real-time across the system to maintain a consistent read of the operation.

It operated with Server-to-Server authentication using API Keys and featured exponential retries for connection drops, which allowed us to prioritize continuity without degrading the operator's experience.

Peripheral zones mostly operated using standard REST requests, and central services distributed events via WebSockets to specific rooms. To facilitate cross-testing, we defined a strict JSON contract and built a diagnostic template in Vanilla JS where the team could quickly document and test their endpoints.

We minimized the use of touchscreens. The system pre-selected the default context based on the zone; the operator only scanned the order receipt and their badge to confirm merchandise movements. The only exception was the final Transfer Point, where tablets were installed for a visual audit alongside the customer.

sections.title: Prioritizing operational fluidity
body: The system successfully eradicated order mix-ups, achieving an average time of 10 minutes from picking to delivery.

However, the traceability data forced us to face the realities of human adoption and business logic. Early on, we noticed that dozens of orders were left "abandoned" for days. When investigating in the field, we discovered two factors: in some cases, it was resistance to change from operators, but in others, it was customers deciding to pick up their merchandise days later.

This project taught me that code must adapt to the available hardware and business rules. The architecture must prioritize operational fluidity over strict data rigidity; and while scalability is important, it shouldn't be an obstacle that paralyzes the operation. The best features are born from interacting with users in their real environment.
